title: Luster dust application
subtitle: dusting and painting with edible metallic and pearlescent powders
excerpt: Luster dust is a fine edible metallic or pearlescent powder that can be applied dry with a soft brush for a subtle sheen, or mixed with a clear spirit or extract and painted on wet for a bright metallic finish. The dry technique suits fondant and gum paste; the wet technique is better for chocolates, macarons, and firm-set surfaces where a stronger effect is wanted.
sourceNotes: Edible lustre powders have been used in professional cake decoration since the 1990s and became widely available to home bakers through specialist cake suppliers in the 2000s. They are commonly made from mica pigments coated with iron oxides and titanium dioxide; the EU and UK classify food-grade mica (E555) as approved for use in food decoration. Dry-brush dusting is a traditional cake technique; wet painting followed as a way to intensify the effect on smooth surfaces.

glossaryTerms.definition: A fine edible powder made from approved food-grade pigments, most commonly mica coated with iron oxides. It produces a metallic or pearlescent sheen when applied to a dry surface. It is distinct from non-edible craft glitters, which must not be used on food.

content.text: Luster dust gives baked decorations a metallic or pearlescent sheen with very little effort. The two application methods, dry dusting and wet painting, produce different results and suit different surfaces. Check the label before buying: only use products labelled edible or food-grade, not cake decoration dusts marketed for display only.
Dry dusting suits fondant-covered cakes, gum paste flowers, and moulded sugar pieces. Dip a soft, dry brush into a small amount of

, tap the ferrule against the edge of the container to dislodge any excess, then brush lightly across the surface using short strokes. The effect is subtle and builds with successive passes. For fondant, work in the direction of any texture or pattern; for gum paste petals, brush from the petal edges inward. This technique is forgiving: you can always add more, but you can't remove it easily without disturbing the surface.

Wet painting produces a much brighter, more opaque metallic finish. Mix a small amount of luster dust with just enough clear spirit (vodka, gin, or clear vanilla extract) to form a smooth, slightly thick paste. A ratio of roughly 1 part dust to 3 to 4 parts liquid is a starting point; the consistency should be similar to a thin watercolour paint. Apply with a firm, flat brush in short strokes on to a firm, dry surface. On chocolate, let the chocolate set fully and be at room temperature before painting; moisture from condensation will cause streaking. The spirit evaporates quickly, leaving a bright metallic finish. Let each coat dry for 1 to 2 minutes before applying a second.

Gold and silver are the most versatile shades. Gold works on warm-coloured decorations (caramel, bronze fondant, dark chocolate); silver reads best on white, ivory, or pale pink surfaces. Pearl dust, which has no metallic hue, adds sheen to any surface without changing the base colour and is a good first purchase if you are new to luster dusts.

attrs.problem: Wet paint application looks streaky or patchy

content.text: Either the surface had condensation on it, or the luster mixture was too thin. Ensure the surface is dry and at room temperature. Make the paint slightly thicker and apply in multiple thin coats rather than one heavy coat.

attrs.problem: Dry dust is patchy and won't brush evenly

content.text: The fondant or gum paste surface is slightly tacky. Refrigerate the piece for 10 minutes to firm the surface, then allow it to come back to room temperature in the air before dusting; the moisture evaporates as it warms and leaves a drier surface for the powder to grip.
